questions.prompt: A linear quadratic regulator chooses the gain \(K\) by
options: minimizing a quadratic cost in the state and the command
copying the open-loop eigenvalues
setting \(K = B\), with no weights
cancelling every entry of \(A\) by hand
questions.explanation: The design starts from the cost, and the gain is whatever that cost selects. Copying the open-loop eigenvalues does nothing. \(K = B\) ignores both weights. Cancelling \(A\) entrywise is not the Riccati solution, even though the closed loop does move the eigenvalues.

questions.prompt: For \(\dot{x} = u\), state weight \(4\), and control weight \(1\), the regulator gain is
questions.explanation: The scalar integrator has \(K = \sqrt{q/r} = \sqrt{4/1} = 2\). The ratio \(q/r = 4\) without the square root is the square of the gain. The reciprocal \(\sqrt{r/q} = 0.5\) inverts the weights. The sum \(4+1 = 5\) is neither weight's job.
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 200 130" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>a state weight beside a control weight</title><text x="28" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">[</text><text x="168" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">]</text><text x="98" y="58" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">Q   R</text></svg>

questions.prompt: For the same integrator \(\dot{x} = u\), state weight \(9\), and control weight \(4\), the gain is
questions.explanation: \(K = \sqrt{9/4} = 1.5\). The Riccati solution \(P = \sqrt{q r} = 6\) is not the gain; dividing by \(r\) is what turns it into \(K\). Reporting \(9\) or \(4\) reports a weight.
questions.figure_alt: A curve that rises and levels off.

questions.prompt: For \(\dot{x} = u\), write the regulator gain in the names \(q\) and \(r\), the state weight and the control weight.
questions.explanation: The Riccati solution is \(\sqrt{q r}\) and the gain divides by \(r\), leaving \(\sqrt{q/r}\). The ratio \(q/r\) misses the root. The reciprocal root \(\sqrt{r/q}\) swaps the weights. The product \(q r\) is the square of \(P\), not the gain.

questions.prompt: For \(\dot{x} = x + u\), state weight \(3\), and control weight \(1\), the positive Riccati solution gives the gain
questions.explanation: The scalar equation is \(p^2 - 2p - 3 = 0\), so the positive solution is \(p = 3\) and \(K = 3\). The negative root \(-1\) is not a positive cost matrix. Reporting the state weight \(3\) happens to match \(K\) here because \(b = r = 1\), and the check is the closed-loop eigenvalue \(1 - 3 = -2\), not the weight. Using \(K = a = 1\) only cancels the open-loop term and leaves a pole at \(0\).

questions.prompt: Put these regulator steps in the order you would do them.
questions.explanation: The weights define the cost, so they come before the equation. The Riccati solution is the matrix the gain formula consumes. The stability check is the property that solution is supposed to deliver. Reading the weight is how you explain the number you got, and it is not a substitute for the solve.

steps: Choose the state weight and the control weight.
Solve the algebraic Riccati equation for the cost matrix.
Set the gain to the inverse of the control weight times B transpose times that matrix.
Check that A minus B K is stable.
Read a larger control weight as a reason to use less command, not more.

questions.prompt: A reachable pair and positive weights are already in hand. One step is wrong.
questions.explanation: A larger \(R\) penalizes the command, so the minimizer uses less of it and the gain gets smaller. The cost, the formula, and the stability claim are the design. The third step has the comparative static backwards.
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 200 130" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>a state weight beside a control weight</title><text x="28" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">[</text><text x="168" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">]</text><text x="98" y="58" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">Q   R</text></svg>
questions.figure_alt: A row of two labels, Q and R.
steps: The cost weights the state with \(Q\) and the command with \(R\).
The gain is \(R^{-1} B^T P\), with \(P\) from the Riccati equation.
Increasing \(R\) makes the command more expensive, so the optimal gain gets larger.
The closed loop is \(A-BK\), and the positive solution makes it stable under the usual definiteness conditions.
reasons: A larger control weight penalizes the command, so the minimizing gain gets smaller.
A larger R increases Q by the same factor.
The Riccati equation does not involve R.

questions.prompt: On an infinite horizon with no explicit constraint, the regulator gain is
options: recomputed from scratch at every time, with a shrinking horizon
a constant matrix, from one algebraic Riccati equation
equal to the open-loop \(A\)
defined only for a single sample
questions.explanation: Time-invariant weights and an infinite horizon make the gain constant. Recomputing on a shrinking horizon is a finite-horizon problem. The gain is not \(A\). A single sample is a one-step problem, not this limit.
questions.figure_alt: A curve that rises and levels off.

questions.prompt: Which statements hold for the infinite-horizon regulator?
options: The gain depends on both the state weight and the control weight.
A larger state weight pushes the design to keep that state smaller.
The algebraic Riccati equation is the Lyapunov equation with the quadratic gain term removed and nothing put in its place.
The optimal gain grows when the control weight grows.
questions.explanation: Both weights enter the gain. Penalizing a state more is what a larger \(Q\) does. The Riccati equation is the Lyapunov equation plus the term that contains the gain, so deleting that term is a different equation. A larger control weight shrinks the gain.

questions.prompt: For \(\dot{x} = u\), state weight \(36\), and control weight \(4\), the gain is
questions.explanation: \(K = \sqrt{36/4} = 3\). The root of the product \(\sqrt{36 \times 4} = 12\) is \(P\), and the gain is \(P/R = 3\). Reporting \(36\) or \(4\) reports a weight. The difference \(36 - 4 = 32\) is not a gain.

questions.prompt: A hard limit on the command is required, and a quadratic weight is not a substitute for it. The design that enforces the limit is
options: a larger control weight, which is the same as a hard stop
the Lyapunov equation with \(Q\) set to zero
a finite-horizon problem that treats the limit as a constraint
the open-loop matrix, left unchanged
questions.explanation: A weight makes large commands expensive and still allows them. A constraint removes the illegal values from the problem, which a receding horizon can do at each sample. The Lyapunov equation does not choose \(K\). Leaving \(A\) unchanged applies no control.
questions.figure_alt: A curve that rises and levels off.

questions.prompt: The same plant is augmented with an integrator of the tracking error before the cost is written. The regulator then
options: drops the integrator, because a quadratic cost cannot see an extra state
uses the control weight as the integrator gain with no solve
is undefined, because the augmented \(A\) has an eigenvalue at \(0\)
returns a gain that includes an entry for the integrator state
questions.explanation: The cost is written on whatever state you hand it, including the integrator state, and the gain has one entry per state. An eigenvalue at \(0\) in the open loop is allowed when the pair stays reachable and the weights keep the solution positive. The control weight is not itself the integrator gain.
